<!-- letterthm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main:introduction}
Assume that \(\mathfrak N=\mathfrak l^e\) with $e>0$. 
Then there exist a number field $L$, a positive-density set $\mathcal P$ of finite
primes of $L$, and an arithmetic progression $\mathfrak V\subset\mathbb Z_{>0}$
such that the following statement is true:
Let $\mathfrak p\in\mathcal P$ and $\mathfrak P$ a prime ideal of $\overline{\mathbb Z}$ lying above $\mathfrak p$. 
Then, for any $\phi\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathfrak V}X_n$, 
there exist $\varepsilon\in\mathcal O_F^\times$ and $\psi\in\widehat\Delta$ such that
\[
 L_f(\phi^\varepsilon\psi)\not\equiv0\pmod{\mathfrak P}.
\]
<!-- end letterthm-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
A Hecke character $\xi$ of $F$ is a continuous homomorphism
\[
  \xi: F^\times \backslash \mathbb{A}_F^\times 
  \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}^\times.
\]
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
The ray class group of modulus $\mathfrak c$ is
\begin{equation*}
  \mathrm{Cl}_F(\mathfrak c)\,:=\,F^\times\backslash \mathbb{A}_F^\times \;\Big/\;
  \left(\mathbb{C}^\times \times 
  \left(1+\widehat{\mathfrak{c}}\right)\right).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:hecke-character-local-extension}
Assume that $\ker(\rho)$ contains the image of $E_F$.
Then, there exists a finite-order Hecke character $\chi$ 
of modulus $\mathfrak c$ such that
\[
 \chi\vert_{O_{\mathfrak c}^\times}=\rho.
\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Applying $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(-,\mathbb{C}^\times)$
to \eqref{eq:ray-class-local-global-exact-sequence},
and using the injectivity of the divisible $\mathbb Z$-module $\mathbb C^\times$, 
we obtain a character $\chi$ satisfying the assertion.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{adel:cuspform:defn} 
A cuspidal automorphic form on $\operatorname{GL}(2)$ 
of parallel weight $(2,2)$, level $\mathfrak N$, and central character $\chi$
is a smooth function 
\[
f:\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_F)\rightarrow \mathbf{L}_2
\]
satisfying the following conditions for any $g\in\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_F)$:
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(1)]                    
    For the Casimir operators $\{D_\tau\mid\tau\in I_F\}$ of 
    $\mathrm{SL}_2$,
    \[
    D_\tau f=0.
    \]
    \item[(2)]
    For all $\gamma\in\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$, 
    $z\in\mathbb A_F^\times$, $u\in U_0(\mathfrak{N})$,
    and $c\in \operatorname{SU}_2(\mathbb{C})$,
    \[
    f(\gamma z g u c,\mathbf{x})=\chi(z)\chi_{\mathfrak N}(d)f(g,c\mathbf{x}),
    \]
    where $d$ is the lower-right entry of the matrix $u$.
    \item[(3)]                
    Let $dx$ be a Haar measure on $F\backslash\mathbb{A}_F$. Then,
    \[
    \int_{F\backslash \mathbb{A}_F}f\left(\left(\begin{matrix} 1 & x \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\right) g\right)dx=0.
    \]
\end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The assumption that the weight is parallel and integral is necessary
for the space of cusp forms to be nonzero~\cite[p.~461]{Hida:1994}.
Under this condition, Hida's rationality results apply to the critical values considered later. 
After normalization by Hida's period and the relevant Gauss and archimedean factors, 
these values are algebraic~\cite[Theorem 8.1]{Hida:1994}.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
The additively twisted partial $L$-function is
\[
L_a(s,f;u):=\frac{1}{\# E_F}\sum_{\alpha\in F^\times}
\frac{a_f(\alpha a\mathfrak{d}_F)\mathbf e_F(\alpha au)}{N( \alpha a\mathfrak{d}_F)^s}.
\]
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{integral:representation:lfunction} 
For $s\in\mathbb{C}$ with $\mathrm{Re}(s)>\frac{3}{2}+\theta$,
\[
|a|_{\mathbb A_F}^{s-1}\int_{E}\widetilde{(f\vert_u)_a}(y)|y|^{2s-2}d^\times y
=
\Gamma_F(s)L_a(s,f;u).
\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Substituting \eqref{modularform:part:expansion} and integrating term by term, we obtain
\begin{align*}
|a|_{\mathbb A_F}^{s-1}\int_{E} \widetilde{(f\vert_u)_a}(y) |y|^{2s-2}d^\times y
&=
|a|_{\mathbb A_F}^s\int_{E}\sum_{\alpha\in F^\times}
a_f(\alpha a\mathfrak{d}_F)\mathbf e_F(\alpha au)| y|^{2s} 
\mathrm{W}(\alpha y)d^\times y 
\\
&=
\frac{\Gamma_F(s)}{\#E_F}\sum_{\alpha\in F^\times}
\frac{a_f(\alpha a\mathfrak{d}_F)\mathbf e_F(\alpha au)}{N(\alpha a\mathfrak{d}_F)^s}
\end{align*}
from \eqref{Whittaker:function:integral}.
Here we have used
\[
N(\alpha a\mathfrak d_F)
=
N(\alpha\mathcal O_F)|a|_{\mathbb A_F}^{-1}D_F.
\]
This proves the proposition.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:normalizer:equation}
We have
\[
 B_{\mathfrak d}^{-1}U_0(\mathfrak N)B_{\mathfrak d}
 =U_0(\mathfrak N).
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
If $v\nmid\mathfrak d$, then
$(B_{\mathfrak d})_v$ is the identity matrix, so there is nothing to prove.
Suppose that $v\mid\mathfrak d$ and
put $e=\operatorname{ord}_v(\mathfrak{d})$.
Note that $\operatorname{ord}_v(\mathfrak{N})=e$.  
Write
\[
 B=(B_{\mathfrak d})_v
 =\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\\varpi_v^e&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 k=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}
 \in U_0(\mathfrak N)_v.
\]
Direct multiplication gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normalizer:calculation}
 B^{-1}kB
 =\begin{pmatrix}
 d&-\varpi_v^{-e}c\\
 -\varpi_v^e b&a
 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
This matrix belongs to $U_0(\mathfrak N)_v$, and hence
$B^{-1}U_0(\mathfrak N)_vB\subseteq U_0(\mathfrak N)_v$.
Since $B=-\varpi_v^e B^{-1}$,
the same calculation gives the reverse inclusion.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
For $\chi\in\mathscr X_{\mathfrak d}$, define the Atkin--Lehner operator
$W_{\mathfrak d}^\chi$
on functions $h:\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb A_F)\to\mathbf{L}_2$ by
\[
 (W_{\mathfrak d}^\chi h) (g)
 :=-\overline\chi_1(\det g)h(gB_{\mathfrak d}).
\]
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:atkin-lehner-unit-obstruction}
The construction requires the local restriction condition~\eqref{eq:atkin-lehner-unit-condition}.
Over a general number field, such an extension exists precisely 
when $\rho_\chi$ is trivial on the group of totally positive units $E_F^+$.
For $F=\mathbb Q$, $E_{\mathbb Q}^+=\{1\}$, so the condition is automatic.  
This explains why the classical Atkin--Lehner construction requires no analogous condition.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:exact-divisor-atkin-lehner-properties}
The Atkin--Lehner operator
\[
 W_{\mathfrak d}^\chi:S_2(\mathfrak N,\chi)
 \longrightarrow S_2(\mathfrak N,\chi')
\]
is well-defined for $\chi\in\mathscr X_\mathfrak d$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
As $\chi_1$ is a Hecke character, the defining formula is left
$\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$-invariant. Right translation by $B_{\mathfrak d}$ 
and multiplication by $\overline{\chi_1}\circ\det$ preserve smoothness, 
the equivariance conditions of the archimedean place, and cuspidality.
Let $z\in\mathbb A_F^\times$,
$k=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in U_0(\mathfrak N)$.
Write $B=B_{\mathfrak d}$ and $k'=B^{-1}kB$.  
Lemma~\ref{lem:normalizer:equation} and 
\eqref{eq:normalizer:calculation} give
\begin{align*}
 f(zgkB)=\chi(z)f(gBk')
 &=\chi(z)\chi_{\mathfrak d}(a)\chi_{\mathfrak N_0}(d)f(gB) \\
 &=\chi(z)\chi_1(\det k)\chi_{\mathfrak N}'(d)f(gB).
\end{align*}
Here, $a,d\in O_{\mathfrak N}^\times$.
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 W_{\mathfrak d}^\chi f(zgk)
 &=-\overline{\chi_1}^2(z)
 \overline{\chi_1}(\det g)\overline{\chi_1}(\det k)f(zgkB) \\
 &=\chi'(z)\chi'_\mathfrak{N}(d)W_{\mathfrak d}f(g).
\end{align*}
This proves the lemma.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:composite-atkin-lehner-involution}
The operator $W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d}$ is an automorphism of the space $S_{\mathfrak d}$. 
More precisely, if $f\in S_2(\mathfrak N,\chi)$, then
\[
 W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d}f
 \in S_2(\mathfrak N,\overline{\chi'})
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 (W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d})^2f= \overline{\chi_1}(\varpi_{\mathfrak N_0}) f.
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Choose $f\in S_2(\mathfrak N,\chi)$ and put
\[
 C:=B_{\mathfrak N}B_{\mathfrak d}^{-1},
 \qquad
 \zeta_\chi:=\overline{\chi_1}(\varpi_{\mathfrak N})
 \chi(\varpi_{\mathfrak d}).
\]
The equality 
$(B_{\mathfrak d})_v=-(\varpi_{\mathfrak d})_v (B_{\mathfrak d}^{-1})_v$ for $v\mid\mathfrak d$ 
gives the alternative formula
\begin{equation}\label{eq:involution:rewrite}
 W_{\mathfrak d} f(g)
 =-\chi(\varpi_{\mathfrak d})
  \overline{\chi_1}(\det g)
  f(gB_{\mathfrak d}^{-1}).
\end{equation}
Then~\eqref{eq:involution:rewrite} gives
\[
 W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d}f(g)
 =\zeta_\chi
  \overline{\chi_2}(\det g)f(gC).
\]
This function has central character
$\overline{\chi'}=\chi_1\overline{\chi_2}$.
Applying the same formula once more, with the compatible auxiliary
characters, gives
\[
 (W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d})^2f
 =  \overline{\chi_1}(\varpi_{\mathfrak N_0})f.
\]
This proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:finite-inversion-matrix-identity}
Assume further that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:assumption:conductor:exponent:large}
\operatorname{ord}_v(\mathfrak c)
\geq
\operatorname{ord}_v(\mathfrak N)
\qquad (v\mid\mathfrak d).
\end{equation}
Then there exists
$A_u\in U_0(\mathfrak N)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:atkin-lehner-twist-matrix-identity}
 B_{\mathfrak M}t(u)
 =\varpi_{\mathfrak c}t(u')B_{\mathfrak N}B_{\mathfrak d}^{-1}A_u
\end{equation}
and the lower-right entry of $(A_u)_v$ is
$(\varpi_{\mathfrak c})_vu_v$ for $v\mid\mathfrak c$ and $1$ otherwise.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
For $v\mid\mathfrak c$, put
\[
  a_{u,v}:=-(\varpi_{\mathfrak c}u'u)_v-(\varpi_{\mathfrak c})_v^{-1}\in O_v
\]
and define
\[
 (A_u)_v=
 \begin{cases}
  \left(\begin{matrix}
    -(\varpi_{\mathfrak c}u')_v&a_{u,v}
    \\
    (\varpi_{\mathfrak c})_v&(\varpi_{\mathfrak c}u)_v
   \end{matrix}\right),
   &v\mid\mathfrak c,\\
   \left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right),
   &\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
By~\eqref{eq:inversion:representative} and the definition of $\mathcal R_{\mathfrak c}$, 
$(A_u)_v\in\mathrm{SL}_2(O_v)$ for each finite place $v$. 
If $v\mid\mathfrak d$, then the lower-left entry $(\varpi_{\mathfrak c})_v$ of $(A_u)_v$
belongs to $\mathfrak N O_v$.
If $v\mid\mathfrak N_0$, then $(A_u)_v=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
Thus $A_u\in U_0(\mathfrak N)$.

At every $v\mid\mathfrak c$, direct multiplication gives
\[
 (\varpi_{\mathfrak c})_vt(u')_{v}(A_u)_v
 =\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\(\varpi_{\mathfrak c})_v^2&(\varpi_{\mathfrak c}^2u)_v\end{pmatrix}
 =\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\(\varpi_{\mathfrak c})_v^2&0\end{pmatrix}t(u)_v.
\]
At $v\mid\mathfrak N_0$, one has $(\varpi_{\mathfrak c})_v=1$, $t(u)_v=t(u')_v=1$,
and $(B_{\mathfrak M})_v=(B_{\mathfrak N})_v$, while
$(B_{\mathfrak d})_v=1$.
At every remaining place all the matrices
are the identity. This proves
\eqref{eq:atkin-lehner-twist-matrix-identity} at every finite place.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:translated-atkin-lehner-identity}
Let $u'$ be as in~\eqref{eq:inversion:representative}. 
Then, for every
$g\in\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb A_F)$,
\[
 \widetilde{W_{\mathfrak M}^{\chi}(f\vert_u)}(g)
 =-
 \frac{
  \chi(\varpi_{\mathfrak c})
  \chi_{\mathfrak d}(\varpi_{\mathfrak c}u)}{
  \overline{\chi_1}(\varpi_{\mathfrak N})
  \chi(\varpi_{\mathfrak d})}
 \overline{\chi_1}(\det g)\,
 \widetilde{
  \left(W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d}f\right)
  \vert_{u'}}(g).
\]
In particular, for every
$y\in\mathbb C^\times$,
\[
 \widetilde{\bigl(W_{\mathfrak M}^{\chi}(f\vert_u)\bigr)_a}(y)
 =-
 \frac{
  \chi(\varpi_{\mathfrak c})
  \chi_{\mathfrak d}(\varpi_{\mathfrak c}u)}{
  \overline{\chi_1}(\varpi_{\mathfrak N})
  \chi(\varpi_{\mathfrak d})}
 \overline{\chi_1}(a)\,
 \widetilde{
  \left(
   \left(W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d}f\right)
   \vert_{u'}
  \right)_a}(y).
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-inversion-matrix-identity} and the
transformation law of $f$ give
\[
 f(gB_{\mathfrak M}t(u))
 =\chi(\varpi_{\mathfrak c})
  \chi_{\mathfrak d}(\varpi_{\mathfrak c}u)
  f(gt(u')B_{\mathfrak N}B_{\mathfrak d}^{-1}).
\]
On the other hand, \eqref{eq:involution:rewrite} gives
\[
 W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d}f(g)
 =\overline{\chi_1}(\varpi_{\mathfrak N})
  \chi(\varpi_{\mathfrak d})
  \overline\chi_2(\det g)
  f(gB_{\mathfrak N}B_{\mathfrak d}^{-1}).
\]
Combining these identities with the definition of
$W_{\mathfrak M}^{\chi}$ proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{functional:equation:lemma}
For a finite idele $a$ of $F$, $y\in\mathbb{C}^\times$, and $s\in\mathbb{C}$,
\[
N(\mathfrak{M})^{\frac{s}{2}}\widetilde{(f\vert_u)_a}(y^{-1})|ay^{-1}|_{\mathbb A_F}^{s-1}
=
N(\mathfrak{M})^{1-\frac{s}{2}}
\widetilde{W_\mathfrak{M}^\chi(f\vert_u)_{\varpi_\mathfrak{M}/a}}(y)|
(\varpi_\mathfrak{M}/a)y|_{\mathbb A_F}^{1-s}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
In this proof, write
\[
B:=\left(\begin{matrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{matrix}\right)
\left(\begin{matrix} \varpi_\mathfrak{M}a^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix}
\right)
\left(\begin{matrix} y & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\right)B_\mathfrak{M}t(u),
\qquad m_v=\mathrm{ord}_v(\mathfrak M).
\]
Here,
$\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right)
\in\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$. 
If $v\mid \mathfrak M$, then
\[
B_v=\left(\begin{matrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{matrix}\right)_v
\left(\begin{matrix} \varpi_v^{m_v}a_v^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\right)
\left(\begin{matrix} 0 & -1 \\ \varpi_v^{m_v} & 0 \end{matrix}\right)t(u_v)
=\varpi_v^{m_v}a_v^{-1}\left(\begin{matrix} a_v & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\right)t(u_v).
\]
Otherwise, 
\[
B_v=(a^{-1}y)_v\left(\begin{matrix} (ay^{-1})_v & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\right)
\left(\begin{matrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{matrix}\right)_v.
\]
In sum,
\[
B
=
a^{-1}\varpi_{\mathfrak{M}}y
\left(\begin{matrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\right)
\left(\begin{matrix} y^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\right)t(u)
\prod_{v\nmid \mathfrak{M}}
\left(\begin{matrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{matrix}\right)_v,
\]
Using the definition of $\widetilde{W_\mathfrak{M}^\chi(f\vert_u)_{\varpi_\mathfrak{M}/a}}$ 
and the above expression for $B$, we obtain
\[
\widetilde{W_\mathfrak{M}^\chi(f\vert_u)_{\varpi_\mathfrak{M}/a}}(y)=
-\widetilde f\left(\left(\begin{matrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\right)
\left(\begin{matrix} y^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\right)t(u)
\left(\begin{matrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{matrix}\right)_\infty
\right).
\]
Together with the property of $f$ and the equation 
\[
N(\mathfrak M)^{1-\frac s2}
\left|(\varpi_{\mathfrak M}/a)y\right|_{\mathbb A_F}^{1-s}
=
N(\mathfrak M)^{\frac s2}
|ay^{-1}|_{\mathbb A_F}^{s-1},
\]
we are done.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{Lftn:analytic:conti} 
The function $\Lambda_a(s,f;u)$ extends to an entire function of
$s\in\mathbb C$ and satisfies
\[
 \Lambda_a(s,f;u)
 =\epsilon_a^\chi(u)
 \Lambda_{\varpi_{\mathfrak M}/a}
 \left(2-s,
 W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d}f;u'\right).
\]
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Put
\[
 E_1:=\{y\in E:|y|\geq1\},
 \qquad
 E_2:=\{y\in E:|y|\leq1\}.
\]
For $\operatorname{Re}(s)>\frac32+\theta$,
Proposition~\ref{integral:representation:lfunction} gives
\[
 \Lambda_a(s,f;u)
 =N(\mathfrak M)^{\frac{s}{2}}
 \left(\int_{E_1}+\int_{E_2}\right)\widetilde{(f\vert_u)_a}(y)
 |ay|_{\mathbb A_F}^{s-1}\,d^\times y.
\]
In the second integral, make the measure-preserving change of variable
$y\mapsto y^{-1}$. Lemma~\ref{functional:equation:lemma}, followed by
Lemma~\ref{lem:translated-atkin-lehner-identity}, gives
\begin{align}\begin{split}\label{eq:lfunction:analytic:continuation}
 \Lambda_a(s,f;u)
 ={}&N(\mathfrak M)^{\frac{s}{2}}
 \int_{E_1}\widetilde{(f\vert_u)_a}(y)
 |ay|_{\mathbb A_F}^{s-1}\,d^\times y\\
 +\epsilon_a^\chi(u)&N(\mathfrak M)^{1-\frac{s}{2}}
 \int_{E_1}
 \widetilde{
 \left(
  \left(W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d}f\right)
  \vert_{u'}
 \right)_{\varpi_{\mathfrak M}/a}}(y)
 \left|(\varpi_{\mathfrak M}/a)y\right|_{\mathbb A_F}^{1-s}
 \,d^\times y.
\end{split}\end{align}
Both integrands are rapidly decreasing on $E_1$. 
Hence the integrals define an entire function of $s$ and give the analytic continuation of $\Lambda_a(s,f;u)$.

The definitions and the compatible choices give
\[
 \epsilon_a^\chi(u)\epsilon_{\varpi_{\mathfrak M}/a}^{\overline{\chi'}}(u')=\chi_1(\varpi_{\mathfrak N_0}).
\]
Apply the substitution
\[
 (s,a,f,u)\longmapsto
 \left(2-s,\varpi_{\mathfrak M}/a,
 W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d}f,u'\right)
\]
to~\eqref{eq:lfunction:analytic:continuation}. Since $u\mapsto u'$ is an involution and
$(W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d})^2=\overline{\chi_1}(\varpi_{\mathfrak N_0})$ 
by Lemma~\ref{lem:composite-atkin-lehner-involution},
multiplication by $\epsilon_a^\chi(u)$ interchanges the two terms in that formula.
This proves the functional equation.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:mellin-transform-extension}
The Mellin transform on the left-hand side of
Proposition~\ref{integral:representation:lfunction} is well defined and
holomorphic for $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$. By Proposition~\ref{Lftn:analytic:conti},
$L_a(s,f;u)$ has an analytic continuation. Since the two sides agree for
$\operatorname{Re}(s)>\frac32+\theta$, the
equality in Proposition~\ref{integral:representation:lfunction} can be extended to the
half-plane $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:additive-approximate-functional-equation}
If the condition~\eqref{eq:assumption:conductor:exponent:large} is satisfied, then for every $y>0$,
\begin{align*}
 L_a(1,f;u)
 ={}&\frac{1}{\#E_F}\sum_{\alpha\in F^\times}
 \frac{a_f(a\alpha\mathfrak d_F)\mathbf e_F(\alpha a u)}
 {N(a\alpha\mathfrak d_F)}
 V_1\left(\frac{N(a\alpha\mathfrak d_F)}{y}\right)\\
 &+\frac{\epsilon_a^\chi(u)}{\#E_F}
 \sum_{\alpha\in F^\times}
 \frac{a_{W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d}f}
 (a'\alpha\mathfrak d_F)\mathbf e_F(\alpha a'u')}
 {N(a'\alpha\mathfrak d_F)}
 V_2\left(
 \frac{N(a'\alpha\mathfrak d_F)y}{N(\mathfrak M)}
 \right).
\end{align*}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Consider
\[
 \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{2+i\mathbb R}
 \Phi(t)\frac{\Gamma_F(1+t)}{\Gamma_F(1)}
 L_a(1+t,f;u)y^t\frac{dt}{t}.
\]
Expanding the $L$-function and integrating term by term gives the
first sum. Shift the contour to $-2+i\mathbb R$. The pole at $t=0$
has residue $L_a(1,f;u)$. Proposition~\ref{Lftn:analytic:conti}
gives
\[
 L_a(1+t,f;u)
 =\epsilon_a^\chi(u)N(\mathfrak M)^{-t}
 \frac{\Gamma_F(1-t)}{\Gamma_F(1+t)}
 L_{\varpi_{\mathfrak M}/a}\left(1-t,W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d}f;u'\right).
\]
Making the change of variable $\alpha\mapsto\beta\alpha$, we obtain
\[
 L_{\varpi_{\mathfrak M}/a}\left(1-t,W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d}f;u'\right)=
 L_{a'}\left(1-t,W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d}f;u'\right).
\]
Use this identity on the shifted contour and then replace $t$ by $-t$.
Expanding this gives the second sum.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:additive-character-multiplicative-coset-average}
Let $b\in O_{\mathfrak l}$. For any $n\geq n_0$,
\[
 \sum_{a\in c\Gamma_{n_0}/\Gamma_n}
 \mathbf e_F\left(\frac{ab}{\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^n}\right)
 =
 \begin{cases}
  \ell^{n-n_0}
  \mathbf e_F\left(\dfrac{bc}{\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^n}\right),
  &b\in\mathfrak l^{n-n_0}O_{\mathfrak l},\\
  0,& \text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Write
\[
 a=c(1+\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{n_0}x),
 \qquad
 x\in O_{\mathfrak l}/\mathfrak l^{n-n_0}O_{\mathfrak l}.
\]
Then the sum can be written as
\[
 \mathbf e_F\left(\frac{bc}{\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^n}\right)
 \sum_{x\;\mathrm{mod}\;\mathfrak l^{n-n_0}}
 \mathbf e_F\left(
  \frac{bcx}{\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{n-n_0}}
 \right).
\]
Applying the orthogonality of characters, then we are done.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:twisted-local-kloosterman-bound}
Let $\rho$ be a finite-order character of $O_{\mathfrak l}^{\times}/\Gamma_e$ for $e>0$. 
Let $b,d\in O_{\mathfrak l}$, not both zero. Set
\[
 r:=\min\{\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak l}(b),
           \operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak l}(d)\}.
\]
If $n-r\geq2\max\{n_0,e\}$, then
\[
 \frac{1}{\ell^{n-n_0}}
 \left|\sum_{a\in c\Gamma_{n_0}/\Gamma_n}
 \rho(a)\mathbf e_F\left(
 \frac{ba+da^{-1}}{\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{n}}\right)\right|
 \leq 2\ell^{n_0-\lfloor(n-r)/2\rfloor}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Put $h=n-r$, $b_0=\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{-r}b$,
and $d_0=\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{-r}d$.
Since $e\leq h$, the summand is invariant under $\Gamma_h$.
Reduction modulo $\mathfrak l^h$ therefore gives
\[
 \frac{1}{\ell^{n-n_0}}
 \sum_{a\in c\Gamma_{n_0}/\Gamma_n}
 \rho(a)\mathbf e_F\left(
 \frac{ba+da^{-1}}{\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{n}}\right)
 =\frac{1}{\ell^{h-n_0}}
 \sum_{a\in c\Gamma_{n_0}/\Gamma_h}
 \rho(a)\mathbf e_F\left(
 \frac{b_0a+d_0a^{-1}}{\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{h}}\right).
\]
Note that $h\geq n_0$. Set $m=\lceil h/2\rceil$ and write
\[
 a=t(1+\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{m}x),\qquad
 t\in c\Gamma_{n_0}/\Gamma_m,\qquad
 x\in O_{\mathfrak l}/\mathfrak l^{h-m}O_{\mathfrak l}.
\]
Since $m\geq e$, we have $\rho(a)=\rho(t)$.
Since $2m\geq h$, we also have
\[
 b_0a+d_0a^{-1}
 \equiv b_0t+d_0t^{-1}
 +\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{m}x(b_0t-d_0t^{-1})
 \pmod{\mathfrak l^h}.
\]
Additive orthogonality rewrites the unnormalized sum modulo
$\mathfrak l^h$ as
\[
 \ell^{h-m}
 \sum_{\substack{t\in c\Gamma_{n_0}/\Gamma_m\\
 b_0t^2\equiv d_0\; (\mathrm{mod}\;\mathfrak l^{h-m})}}
 \rho(t)\mathbf e_F\left(
 \frac{b_0t+d_0t^{-1}}{\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{h}}\right).
\]
At least one of $b_0,d_0$ is a unit, and $h-m\geq1$.
If exactly one is a unit, the congruence has no solution.
Otherwise, since $\ell$ is odd, it has at most two solutions
modulo $\mathfrak l^{h-m}$.
These lift to at most $2\ell^{2m-h}$ classes modulo $\mathfrak l^m$.
The unnormalized sum is thus bounded by $2\ell^m$.
Dividing by $\ell^{h-n_0}$ proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:additive-dual-kloosterman-bound}
\begin{comment}
   
                
                                           
                                  
                              
  
                             
  
                                               
                                         
  
               
\end{comment}
For fixed $\alpha\in \mathfrak d_F^{-1}\setminus\{0\}$ and all sufficiently large $n$,
we have the bound
\[
 \left|\mathcal A_n^\chi(c;\alpha,\beta)\right|
 \ll_{\ell,n_0,\alpha}\ell^{-n/2}
\]
which holds uniformly in $c\in O_{\mathfrak l}^{\times}$ and $\beta\in (b_{\mathfrak M}\mathfrak d_F)^{-1}$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
We have
\[
 \epsilon_1^\chi\left(\frac{a}{\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^n}\right)
 =-\overline\chi(\varpi_{\mathfrak c})\chi(a).
\]
Since $\ell$ splits in $F$ and $b_{\mathfrak M}$ is a local unit,
both $\alpha$ and $\beta b_{\mathfrak M}$ are integral at $\mathfrak l$,
and $\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak l}(\beta b_{\mathfrak M})
=\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak l}(\beta)$.
Note that the restriction of $\chi$ to $\Gamma_e$ is trivial, 
so we apply Lemma~\ref{lem:twisted-local-kloosterman-bound} with
$b=-\alpha$ and $d=-\beta b_{\mathfrak M}$.
If $n\geq\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak l}(\alpha)+2\max\{n_0,e\}$, then
the bound holds uniformly in $\beta$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:additive-average-vertical-limit}
Let $c\in O_{\mathfrak l}^{\times}$ and
$\alpha\in\mathfrak d_F^{-1}\setminus\{0\}$.  Then
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}L_n^{\mathrm{av}}(f;c,\alpha)
 =\frac{1}{\#E_F}
  \frac{a_f(\alpha\mathfrak d_F)}
       {N(\alpha\mathfrak d_F)}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The proof closely follows the proof of
\cite[Proposition~6.2]{Kwon:2023}.  We briefly recall the main steps.
Apply \eqref{eq:additive-average-two-pieces} and choose the auxiliary
parameter $y=y_n$ as in the proof cited above.  In
\eqref{eq:additive-average-first-piece},
Lemma~\ref{lem:additive-character-multiplicative-coset-average} shows
that only the terms satisfying
\[
 \beta\in (\alpha+\mathfrak l^{n-n_0}O_{\mathfrak l})\cap\mathfrak d_F^{-1}
\]
can contribute.  Among them, the term 
\[
 \frac{1}{\#E_F}
 \frac{a_f(\alpha\mathfrak d_F)}
      {N(\alpha\mathfrak d_F)}
 V_1\left(\frac{N(\alpha\mathfrak d_F)}{y_n}\right)
\]
at $\beta=\alpha$ is the main term.
This converges to the asserted main term as $n\to\infty$ since
$V_1(x)\to1$ as $x\to0^+$.
After removing this term, the remaining part of
\eqref{eq:additive-average-first-piece} and the whole of
\eqref{eq:additive-average-second-piece} tend to zero.  Indeed, one
uses Lemma~\ref{lem:additive-character-multiplicative-coset-average},
the triangle-inequality argument of
\cite[Proposition~6.2]{Kwon:2023}, the bound of Blomer--Brumley
\cite{BlomerBrumley:2011} for the coefficients of $f$ and
$W_{\mathfrak N}W_{\mathfrak d}f$, and Abel summation.  For the dual
sum, one additionally applies
Proposition~\ref{prop:additive-dual-kloosterman-bound} to
$\mathcal A_n^\chi(c;\alpha,\beta)$, then the result follows.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{universal:coefficient:theorem:homology}
Assume that $R$ is a principal ideal domain. Then we have the following
short exact sequence:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow{r} &
H_j(C_\bullet)\otimes_R A \arrow{r}{\beta_A} &
H_j(C_\bullet\otimes_R A) \arrow{r} &
\operatorname{Tor}_1^R\!\bigl(H_{j-1}(C_\bullet),A\bigr)
\arrow{r} & 0
\end{tikzcd}.
\end{equation*}
We adopt the convention that \(H_{-1}(C_\bullet)=0\).
The sequence is natural in \(C_\bullet\) and \(A\).
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{universal:coefficient:theorem:cohomology}
Assume that $R$ is a principal ideal domain. Then there is a short exact sequence:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \arrow{r} 
& 
\mathrm{Ext}^1_R\left(H_{j-1}(C_\bullet),A\right) \arrow{r} 
& 
H^j(C_A^\bullet) \arrow{r}{\mathcal{D}_\cap} 
& 
\mathrm{Hom}_R\left(H_j(C_\bullet),A\right) \arrow{r} 
&
0
\end{tikzcd}.
\end{equation*}
We adopt the convention that $H_{-1}(C_\bullet)=0$. The sequence is natural in \(C_\bullet\) and \(A\).
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{remark:borel-moore-relative-chain-model}
Suppose that $Y$ admits a Borel--Serre compactification
$\overline Y^{\rm BS}$. Then there are canonical identifications:
\[
H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,R)
\simeq
H_j(\overline Y^{\rm BS},\partial\overline Y^{\rm BS};R),
\qquad
H_{\rm c}^j(Y,R)
\simeq
H^j(\overline Y^{\rm BS},\partial\overline Y^{\rm BS};R).
\]
Consequently, Borel--Moore homology is computed by the free relative
chain complex
\[
C_\bullet(\overline Y^{\rm BS},
\partial\overline Y^{\rm BS};R),
\]
and compactly supported cohomology is computed by its dual. Thus the
universal coefficient theorems apply to these theories through this
relative model.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{parabolic:duality:pairing:lemma}
Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain. Suppose that
\[
\operatorname{Tor}_1^{\mathbb{Z}}
\bigl(H_{j-1}(Y,\mathbb{Z}),A\bigr)
=
\operatorname{Tor}_1^{\mathbb{Z}}
\bigl(H_{j-1}^{\rm BM}(Y,\mathbb{Z}),A\bigr)=0,
\]
\[
\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathbb{Z}}^1
\bigl(H_{j-1}(Y,\mathbb{Z}),A\bigr)
=
\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathbb{Z}}^1
\bigl(H_{j-1}^{\rm BM}(Y,\mathbb{Z}),A\bigr)=0,
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Ext}_A^1\left(
\operatorname{coker}\left(H_j(Y,A)\longrightarrow
H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,A)\right),A\right)=0.
\]
Then the parabolic pairing induces an isomorphism
\[
\mathcal{D}_\cap:H^j_!(Y,A)\;\longrightarrow\;
\operatorname{Hom}_A\bigl(H_j^!(Y,A),A\bigr),
\qquad \delta\longmapsto(c\mapsto c\cap\delta).
\]
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Write $V^\vee:=\operatorname{Hom}_A(V,A)$
for an $A$-module $V$. Apply
Lemma~\ref{universal:coefficient:theorem:homology} over
$\mathbb{Z}$ with coefficients in $A$. The first vanishing
assumption implies that the following scalar-extension maps
are isomorphisms
\[
\beta_A:H_j(Y,\mathbb{Z})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}A
\xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }H_j(Y,A), \qquad
\beta_A^{\rm BM}:H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,\mathbb{Z})
\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}A
\xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,A).  
\]
Tensor--Hom adjunction, 
evaluation maps and the preceding scalar-extension isomorphisms give the commutative diagrams
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
H^j(Y,A) \arrow{r}{\mathcal D_\cap}
\arrow{d}{\mathcal D_\cap^{\mathbb Z}} &
H_j(Y,A)^\vee \arrow{d}{\beta_A^\vee} \\
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(H_j(Y,\mathbb Z),A)
\arrow{r}{\operatorname{adj}} &
\left(H_j(Y,\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}A\right)^\vee
\end{tikzcd}
\]
and
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
H_{\rm c}^j(Y,A) \arrow{r}{\mathcal D_\cap}
\arrow{d}{\mathcal D_\cap^{\mathbb Z}} &
H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,A)^\vee \arrow{d}{(\beta_A^{\rm BM})^\vee} \\
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,\mathbb Z),A)
\arrow{r}{\operatorname{adj}} &
\left(H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}A\right)^\vee
\end{tikzcd}.
\]
The vertical maps $\mathcal D_\cap^{\mathbb Z}$ are isomorphisms
for both the ordinary and the Borel--Moore settings
by Lemma~\ref{universal:coefficient:theorem:cohomology} with the second vanishing assumption.
In the ordinary case, for
$[\delta]\in H^j(Y,A)$, $[c]\in H_j(Y,\mathbb Z)$, and $a\in A$,
commutativity gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:eval:map:compatible}
\mathcal D_\cap([\delta])\left(\beta_A([c]\otimes a)\right)
=a\,\mathcal D_\cap^{\mathbb Z}([\delta])([c])
=a\,\delta(c).
\end{equation}
The analogous identity in the Borel--Moore setting holds for
$[c]\in H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,\mathbb Z)$ and
$[\delta]\in H_{\rm c}^j(Y,A)$, with $\beta_A$ replaced by
$\beta_A^{\rm BM}$.
Let
\[
f_A:H_j(Y,A)\longrightarrow H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,A),
\qquad
\iota_A:H_{\rm c}^j(Y,A)\longrightarrow H^j(Y,A)
\]
be the natural maps.
The compatibility~\eqref{eq:eval:map:compatible} gives
\[
\mathcal D_\cap(\iota_A(\delta))(x)
=f_A^\vee\bigl(\mathcal D_\cap(\delta)\bigr)(x)
\]
for every $x\in H_j(Y,A)$ and $\delta\in H_{\rm c}^j(Y,A)$.
Hence the following diagram commutes, and its horizontal maps are
isomorphisms:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:comm:diag:parabolic}
\begin{tikzcd}
H_{\rm c}^j(Y,A) \arrow{r}{\mathcal D_\cap}
\arrow{d}{\iota_A} &
H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,A)^\vee \arrow{d}{f_A^\vee} \\
H^j(Y,A) \arrow{r}{\mathcal D_\cap} & H_j(Y,A)^\vee
\end{tikzcd}.  
\end{equation}
Put $I:=\operatorname{im}(f_A)=H_j^!(Y,A)$ and
$Q:=\operatorname{coker}(f_A)$. Applying $\vee$ to the exact sequence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exact:seq:bm}
  0\longrightarrow I\rightarrow H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,A)
\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow0
\end{equation}
and using the last vanishing assumption that $\operatorname{Ext}_A^1(Q,A)=0$, 
we find that the following restriction map is surjective:
\[
H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,A)^\vee\longrightarrow I^\vee.
\]
Moreover, the surjection $H_j(Y,A)\to I$ induces an
injection $I^\vee\hookrightarrow H_j(Y,A)^\vee$, and
\[
f_A^\vee=
\left(I^\vee\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow H_j(Y,A)^\vee\right)
\circ
\left(H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,A)^\vee\longrightarrow I^\vee\right).
\]
Consequently, the image of $f_A^\vee$ is canonically isomorphic to
$I^\vee$. The commutative diagram~\eqref{eq:comm:diag:parabolic} therefore
induces an isomorphism
\[
H_!^j(Y,A)=\operatorname{im}(\iota_A)
\xrightarrow{\;\simeq\;}
\operatorname{im}(f_A^\vee)
\xrightarrow{\;\simeq\;}
I^\vee
=
\operatorname{Hom}_A\bigl(H_j^!(Y,A),A\bigr).
\]
This isomorphism sends \(\delta\in H_!^j(Y,A)\) to the functional
$c\longmapsto c\cap\delta$.
It is therefore the parabolic pairing map \(\mathcal D_\cap\).
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{universal:coefficient:parabolic:dedekind}
Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain and let $k$ be a field equipped with an
$A$-algebra structure. Assume that, for each $B\in\{A,k\}$,
\[
\operatorname{Tor}_1^{\mathbb{Z}}\left(H_{j-1}(Y,\mathbb{Z}),B\right)=
\operatorname{Tor}_1^{\mathbb{Z}}\left(H_{j-1}^{\rm BM}(Y,\mathbb{Z}),B\right)=0,
\]
and that
\[
\operatorname{Tor}_1^A\left(
\operatorname{coker}\left(H_j(Y,A)\longrightarrow
H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,A)\right),k\right)=0.
\]
Then the scalar-extension map
\[
H_j^!(Y,A)\otimes_Ak
\longrightarrow H_j^!(Y,k)
\]
is a well-defined isomorphism.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{universal:coefficient:theorem:homology} and the first vanishing assumption, 
the scalar-extension maps 
\[\beta_A^{\mathbb Z}: H_j(Y,\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}A\longrightarrow H_j(Y,A),
\qquad
\beta_k^{\mathbb Z}:H_j(Y,\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k\longrightarrow H_j(Y,k)
\]
are isomorphisms.
Therefore, the following diagram is commutative, and its horizontal maps are isomorphisms:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
\left(H_j(Y,\mathbb{Z})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}A\right)\otimes_A k
\arrow{r}{\beta_A^{\mathbb Z}\otimes 1}\arrow{d}{\operatorname{assoc}} &
H_j(Y,A)\otimes_A k \arrow{d}{\beta_k} \\
H_j(Y,\mathbb{Z})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}k
\arrow{r}{\beta_k^{\mathbb Z}} & H_j(Y,k)
\end{tikzcd}.
\]
Here, $\operatorname{assoc}$ is the canonical associativity
isomorphism given by
\[
\operatorname{assoc}\left(([c]\otimes a)\otimes\lambda\right)
=[c]\otimes(a\lambda),
\]
and $\beta_k$ is the scalar-extension map.
$\beta_k$ is therefore an isomorphism. 
The same argument for Borel--Moore homology shows that 
the scalar-extension map
\[
\beta_k^{\rm BM}:H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,A)\otimes_A k
\longrightarrow H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,k)
\]
is an isomorphism. Let
\[
f_A:H_j(Y,A)\longrightarrow H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,A),
\qquad
f_k:H_j(Y,k)\longrightarrow H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,k)
\]
be the natural maps. By naturality, the scalar-extension maps fit into the commutative
diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
H_j(Y,A)\otimes_A k \arrow{r}{\beta_k}\arrow{d}{f_A\otimes 1} &
H_j(Y,k) \arrow{d}{f_k} \\
H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,A)\otimes_A k
\arrow{r}{\beta_k^{\rm BM}} &
H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,k)
\end{tikzcd}.
\]
Tensoring the exact sequence~\eqref{eq:exact:seq:bm}
with $k$ and using the last vanishing assumption $\operatorname{Tor}_1^A(\mathrm{Coker}(f_A),k)=0$, 
we obtain an injection
\[
H_j^!(Y,A)\otimes_A k\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow
H_j^{\rm BM}(Y,A)\otimes_A k.
\]
Its image is precisely $\operatorname{im}(f_A\otimes 1)$. By the second
commutative diagram and its two horizontal isomorphisms, the latter
image is carried isomorphically onto
$\operatorname{im}(f_k)=H_j^!(Y,k)$.
Thus, the induced map in the statement is a well-defined isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
For each cusp \(s\) of
\(Y^t(U)\), choose a cusp neighborhood
\[
  U_s\simeq
  (y_0,\infty)\times\Gamma_s\backslash\mathbb R^{d-1},
  \qquad d=\dim Y^t(U).
\]
Here, \(y\) is the height coordinate at \(s\); thus \(y\to\infty\)
means approaching the cusp.
Choose a closed differential form \(\omega\) representing a
class in \(H_!^1(Y^t(U),\mathbb C)\). 
Then \(\omega\) is rapidly decreasing in the height coordinate at every cusp.
There is therefore a canonical smooth function \(\theta_s\) on \(U_s\) satisfying
\[
  d\theta_s=\omega|_{U_s},
  \qquad
  \lim_{y\to\infty}\theta_s(y,x)=0.
\]
Choose a smooth function \(\phi_s\) supported in \(U_s\) and equal to
\(1\) for sufficiently large \(y\). Then
\[
  \omega':=\omega-d\left(\sum_s\phi_s\theta_s\right)
\]
is compactly supported, and we define
\[
  \iota_t([\omega])
  :=
  \left[
    \omega'
  \right]
  \in H_{\mathrm c}^1(Y^t(U),\mathbb C).
\]
The resulting class is independent of the cusp neighborhoods and
cutoff functions. $\iota_t$ is compatible with the Hecke action; 
for details, see \cite[\S3]{Hida:1993} and \cite[\S2]{Hida:1999}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{eichler:shimura:harder}
The direct sum of the maps $\delta_i$ induces a Hecke-equivariant isomorphism
\[
\bigoplus_{\chi_0=\rho}
S_2(\mathfrak N,\chi)
\xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }
\bigoplus_{i=1}^{h_F}H_!^1\left(Y_0^i(\mathfrak N),\mathcal L_i(\rho,\mathbb C)\right)
\xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }
H_!^1\left(Y_0(\mathfrak N),\mathcal L(\rho,\mathbb C)\right).
\]
Here, the leftmost direct sum is over the finite-order Hecke characters \(\chi\) of modulus $\mathfrak N$
satisfying \(\chi_0=\rho\).
On the \(\chi\)-summand, the first map sends \(f\) to \((\delta_i(f))_{i=1}^{h_F}\). 
The second map is induced by~\eqref{eq:arith:mfd:disjoint:union}.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:hecke-character-local-extension}, the assumption on $\rho$ 
allows $\rho$ to be extended to a finite-order Hecke character of modulus $\mathfrak N$.
Hence the indexing set of the direct sum $\bigoplus_{\chi_0=\rho}$ is nonempty.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:eichler-shimura-u1-componentwise}
The direct sum of the maps $\delta_i$ induces a Hecke-equivariant isomorphism
\[
 \bigoplus_{\chi}S_2(\mathfrak N,\chi)
 \xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }
 \bigoplus_{i=1}^{h_F}H_!^1(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),\mathbb C)
 \xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }
 H_!^1(Y_1(\mathfrak N),\mathbb C),
 \qquad
 f\longmapsto(\delta_i(f))_{i=1}^{h_F},
\]
where the sum is over the finite-order Hecke characters $\chi$ of
modulus $\mathfrak N$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
For each character $\rho$ of $\widehat{\mathcal O}_F^\times$ trivial on $1+\widehat{\mathfrak N}$ and $E_F$,
Proposition~\ref{eichler:shimura:harder} and~\eqref{eq:localsys:eigensp} 
give the identification between the sum of cusp form spaces and the $\rho$-eigenspace 
$H_!^1(Y_1(\mathfrak N),\mathbb C)[\rho]$. Taking the sum over $\rho$ gives the asserted isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
As in Subsection~\ref{subsec:atkin-lehner-func-eq}, cusp forms with
distinct central characters are linearly independent. Hence the direct
sum in Proposition~\ref{prop:eichler-shimura-u1-componentwise} may be
identified with the ordinary sum
\[
\bigoplus_{\chi} S_2(\mathfrak N,\chi)
=
\sum_{\chi} S_2(\mathfrak N,\chi)
\]
inside the space of functions
$\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb A_F)\to\mathbf L_2$.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:hoch:serre}
Let $A$ be a coefficient ring in which $\#E_F$ is invertible. Then the pullback of the orbifold covering 
$Y^i(\mathfrak N)\longrightarrow Y_1^i(\mathfrak N)$ induces an isomorphism
\[
H^j(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),A)
\xrightarrow{\;\simeq\;}
H^j(Y^i(\mathfrak N),A)^{E_F}
\]
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The assertion follows from the Hochschild--Serre spectral sequence of the $E_F$-covering 
(see~\eqref{eq:gamma1-bargamma1-unit-sequence}).
Indeed, as $\#E_F$ is invertible in $A$, the $E_F$-invariant functor is exact, 
so the sequence degenerates at $E_2$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:degree-one-bm-cokernel}
Let $r$ be the number of cusps of $Y_1^i(\mathfrak N)$.
Then there is a canonical identification
\[
\operatorname{coker}\left(H_1(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),A)\longrightarrow H_1^{\rm BM}(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),A)\right)
\cong
\ker\left(A^r\xrightarrow{\ (a_s)_s\mapsto\sum_s a_s\ }A\right).
\]
In particular, this cokernel is a free $A$-module of rank $r-1$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Put $Y=Y_1^i(\mathfrak N)$.
The boundary exact sequence~\eqref{boundary:exact:sequence} gives
\[
H_1(Y,A)\longrightarrow H_1^{\rm BM}(Y,A)
\longrightarrow H_0(\partial\overline Y^{\rm BS},A)
\longrightarrow H_0(Y,A).
\]
Since $Y$ is connected and its boundary has $r$ connected components,
the last map is the summation map $A^r\to A$.
Exactness gives the identification. Since $r\geq 1$, its kernel
is isomorphic to $A^{r-1}$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:parabolic-homology-base-change}
Let $k$ be a field equipped with an $A$-algebra structure.
Scalar extension induces an isomorphism
\[
H_1^!(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),A)\otimes_A k
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
H_1^!(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),k).
\]
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:degree-one-bm-cokernel}
and the connectedness and noncompactness of $Y_1^i(\mathfrak N)$, all the hypotheses of
Lemma~\ref{universal:coefficient:parabolic:dedekind} are satisfied for
$j=1$. The result follows from that lemma.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{dualmap:isom}
For the parabolic pairing for homology and cohomology with coefficient $A$,
the map 
\[\mathcal{D}_\cap:
H \;\longrightarrow\; M^\vee
\]
is an isomorphism. Furthermore, if $A$ is a field, 
then the parabolic pairing is perfect.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Put $Y=Y_1^i(\mathfrak N)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:degree-one-bm-cokernel}
and the connectedness and noncompactness of $Y$, all the hypotheses of
Lemma~\ref{parabolic:duality:pairing:lemma} are satisfied for $j=1$.
That lemma gives the asserted isomorphism. If $A$ is a field, 
then $M$ is finite-dimensional and hence canonically
isomorphic to its double dual. Therefore the parabolic pairing is perfect.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{double:coset:operator:representatives}
Every double coset in the quotient space
\[
\Gamma\backslash
\Gamma\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&q\end{pmatrix}\Gamma
/\Gamma_s
\]
has a representative in the set
\[
\left\{
g_s\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&q\end{pmatrix}g_s^{-1},\ 
g_s\begin{pmatrix}q&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}g_s^{-1}
\right\}.
\]
Both elements fix \(s\).
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
For this proof, put
\[
D:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&q\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
D^\vee:=\begin{pmatrix}q&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathfrak b=\mathfrak a_i.
\]
Every class is represented by $D\gamma$ for some
$\gamma=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\Gamma$.
Write
\[
\gamma g_s=
\begin{pmatrix}a_s&b_s\\ c_s&d_s\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:membership:entry}
a_s\in\mathfrak{a}_s,\qquad
b_s\in\mathfrak{b}\mathfrak{a}_s^{-1},\qquad
c_s\in\mathfrak{b}^{-1}\mathfrak{a}_s,\qquad
d_s\in\mathfrak{a}_s^{-1},  
\end{equation}
and
$a_sd_s-b_sc_s=u$, where
$u:=\det(\gamma)\in\mathcal{O}_F^\times$. It follows that the integral ideals
$a_s\mathfrak{a}_s^{-1}$ and $c_s\mathfrak{b}\mathfrak{a}_s^{-1}$ are coprime.
We now distinguish two cases.

Suppose first that $a_s\mathfrak{a}_s^{-1}$ is coprime to
$q\mathcal{O}_F$.
Then
\[
a_s\mathfrak{a}_s^{-1}
+q c_s\mathfrak{b}\mathfrak{a}_s^{-1}=\mathcal{O}_F,
\]
so there exist $e\in\mathfrak{a}_s^{-1}$ and
$f\in\mathfrak{b}\mathfrak{a}_s^{-1}$ such that
$a_s e-qc_s f=1$.  Set
\[
t:=(1-q)b_s e
\in\mathfrak{b}\mathfrak{a}_s^{-2}\mathfrak{N},
\qquad
u_{s,t}:=g_s\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}g_s^{-1}.
\]
Explicitly,
\[
u_{s,t}=
\begin{pmatrix}
1-tx_sz_s&tx_s^2\\
-tz_s^2&1+tx_sz_s
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its diagonal entries lie in $\mathcal{O}_F$, its upper-right entry lies in
$\mathfrak{b}$, and its lower-left entry lies in
$\mathfrak{b}^{-1}\mathfrak{N}$.  Since $\det(u_{s,t})=1$ and
$u_{s,t}$ fixes $s$, we have $u_{s,t}\in\Gamma_s$.  Let
\[
H_{s,1}:=g_sDg_s^{-1},
\qquad
\gamma_1:=H_{s,1}u_{s,t}\gamma^{-1}D^{-1}.
\]
Since
\[
\gamma^{-1}
=u^{-1}g_s
\begin{pmatrix}d_s&-b_s\\-c_s&a_s\end{pmatrix},
\]
we first obtain
\[
\gamma_1
=u^{-1}g_s
\begin{pmatrix}
d_s-tc_s&q^{-1}(-b_s+ta_s)\\
-qc_s&a_s
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Substituting $t=(1-q)b_s e$ and using
$a_s e-qc_s f=1$ gives
\[
\gamma_1=
u^{-1}
\begin{pmatrix}
d+c_s(1-q)(y_s-b_s e x_s)
&b_sc_s f x_s+a_s(y_s-b_s e x_s)\\
-c+c_s(1-q)(w_s-b_s e z_s)
&b_sc_s f z_s+a_s(w_s-b_s e z_s)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Here
\[
y_s-b_s e x_s\in\mathfrak{b}\mathfrak{a}_s^{-1},
\qquad
w_s-b_s e z_s\in\mathfrak{a}_s^{-1},
\qquad
f\in\mathfrak{b}\mathfrak{a}_s^{-1}.
\]
Using also the memberships~\eqref{eq:membership:entry},
$x_s\in\mathfrak a_s$ and $z_s\in\mathfrak b^{-1}\mathfrak a_s$,
the displayed formula for $\gamma_1$ and the fact that $u$ is a unit show that
\[
\gamma_1\in
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathcal O_F&\mathfrak b\\
\mathfrak b^{-1}\mathfrak N&\mathcal O_F
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Moreover, $\det(\gamma_1)=u^{-1}\in\mathcal O_F^\times$.
It remains to check the congruence condition on the lower-right entry.
The upper-left entry is congruent to $\det(\gamma_1)$ modulo $\mathfrak N$.
Consequently, the lower-right entry belongs to $1+\mathfrak N$.
Hence $\gamma_1\in\Gamma$.
The identity
$\gamma_1D\gamma=H_{s,1}u_{s,t}$ therefore yields
\[
\Gamma D\gamma\Gamma_s=\Gamma H_{s,1}\Gamma_s.
\]
Suppose now that $a_s\mathfrak{a}_s^{-1}\subseteq q\mathcal{O}_F$.  Write
$a_s=qa_s'$ with $a_s'\in\mathfrak{a}_s$, and let
\[
H_{s,2}:=g_sD^\vee g_s^{-1},
\qquad
\gamma_2:=H_{s,2}\gamma^{-1}D^{-1}.
\]
A direct calculation gives
\[
\gamma_2=
u^{-1}
\begin{pmatrix}
d+(q-1)d_s x_s&(1-q)a_s'y_s-b\\
-c+(q-1)d_s z_s&a+(1-q)a_s'w_s
\end{pmatrix}\in
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathcal O_F&\mathfrak b\\
\mathfrak b^{-1}\mathfrak N& 1+\mathfrak{N}
\end{pmatrix}
\]
and $\det(\gamma_2)=u^{-1}$.
This shows that $\gamma_2\in\Gamma$.  Hence
\[
\Gamma D\gamma\Gamma_s=\Gamma H_{s,2}\Gamma_s.
\]
The two cases are exhaustive because $q\mathcal{O}_F$ is prime, proving the
claim.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{hecke:action:boundary:cohom}
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity equipped with the trivial $\operatorname{GL}_2(F)$-action.
If $\mathfrak{a}_i$ is coprime to $q\mathcal O_F$, then
\[
T_{q\mathcal{O}_F}=N(q\mathcal O_F)+1
\]
on $H^0(\partial \overline{Y_1^i(\mathfrak{N})}^{\mathrm{BS}},A)$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Put $\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak a_i$ and
\(
D=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&q\end{smallmatrix}\right).
\)
Under the canonical decomposition
\[
H^0(\partial \overline{Y_1^i(\mathfrak{N})}^{\mathrm{BS}},A)
\cong
\bigoplus_{s\,:\,\textrm{cusps}}H^0(\Gamma_s,A),
\]
write $c=(c_s)_s$.  Fix a cusp $s$, and choose decompositions
\[
\Gamma D\Gamma
=\bigsqcup_i\Gamma\beta_i\Gamma_s,
\qquad
\Gamma\beta_i\Gamma_s
=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^{m_i}\Gamma\beta_i\pi_{ij},
\quad \pi_{ij}\in\Gamma_s.
\]
Hida's boundary formula \cite[(3.1a)--(3.1c)]{Hida:1993} gives
\[
(T_{q\mathcal O_F}c)_s
=\sum_i
c_{\beta_i(s)}\bigm|
[\Gamma_{\beta_i(s)}\beta_i\Gamma_s].
\]
By Proposition~\ref{double:coset:operator:representatives}, the $\beta_i$ may
be chosen so that $\beta_i(s)=s$.  Hida's result
\cite[Lemma~3.3]{Hida:1993} identifies 
\(\Gamma_{\beta_i(s)}\beta_i\Gamma_s
=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^{m_i}
\Gamma_{\beta_i(s)}\beta_i\pi_{ij}.\)
Since $A$ has
trivial action, each of these cosets acts as the identity on $H^0(\Gamma_s,A)$.
Therefore
\[
(T_{q\mathcal O_F}c)_s
=\sum_i m_i c_s
=\left|\Gamma\backslash\Gamma D\Gamma\right|c_s.
\]
It remains to compute the degree of the Hecke correspondence. 
Since $q\mathcal O_F$ is coprime to $\mathfrak b$,
\[
\Gamma D\Gamma
=\Gamma\begin{pmatrix}q&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\sqcup
\bigsqcup_{\beta\in\mathfrak b/q\mathfrak b}
\Gamma\begin{pmatrix}1&\beta\\0&q\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Hence
\(
\left|\Gamma\backslash\Gamma D\Gamma\right|
=1+\left|\mathfrak b/q\mathfrak b\right|
=N(q\mathcal O_F)+1.
\)
Since \(s\) was arbitrary, 
\(T_{q\mathcal O_F}\) acts as multiplication by \(N(q\mathcal O_F)+1\).
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{defn:compact:class:lifting}

For a class $\eta$ in $H^1_!(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),A)$, 
let $\eta'\in H_{\mathrm c}^1(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),A)$ be a lift of $\eta$, and set
\[
\eta_{\mathrm c}:=\mathcal E_q\eta'\in H_{\mathrm c}^1(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),A).
\]
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:canonical-compact-lift}
The map
\[
(-)_{\operatorname{c}}:H_!^1(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),A)
\longrightarrow
H_{\mathrm c}^1(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),A),
\qquad
\eta\longmapsto\eta_{\mathrm c},
\]
is a well-defined \(A\)-linear map. Furthermore,
\[
(H^1_{\operatorname{c}}\to H^1_!)\circ (-)_{\operatorname{c}}=\mathcal E_q.
\]
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Put $Y=Y_1^i(\mathfrak N)$.
If \(\eta'\) and \(\eta''\) map to \(\eta\), then
\(\eta'-\eta''\) lies in the image of the Hecke-equivariant map
\[
H^0(\partial\overline{Y}^{\mathrm{BS}},A)
\longrightarrow H_{\mathrm c}^1(Y,A).
\]
Lemma~\ref{hecke:action:boundary:cohom} shows that
\(\mathcal E_q\) annihilates this image. Hence
\[
\mathcal E_q\eta'=\mathcal E_q\eta''.
\]
The final assertion follows from the Hecke equivariance of
\(H_{\mathrm c}^1\to H_!^1\).
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:auto:sym}
Let $\lambda_{u,i}$
be the well-defined functional~\eqref{eq:symbol:defining:functional}.
Define the \emph{automorphic symbol} associated with $u\in\mathcal R_{\mathfrak c}$ by
\[
\Upsilon_i(u)
:=s_M\!\left((\mathcal D_\cap^\vee)^{-1}
(\lambda_{u,i})\right)
\in H_1^!(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),A).
\]
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{remark:automorphic-symbol-choice-independency}
We can check that the automorphic symbol does not depend
on the choice of $\alpha_{u,i}$: Let us choose another element
$\beta_{u,i}$. 
By equation~\eqref{eq:semi:normalization}, 
the two induced maps differ by the action of an element of
$\Gamma_1^i(\mathfrak N)$.  This action is trivial on
$Y_1^i(\mathfrak N)$, and hence the functional
\eqref{eq:symbol:defining:functional} is independent of the choice.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:unit-action-automorphic-symbol}
Let $\varepsilon\in E_F$ and $u\in\mathcal R_{\mathfrak c}$.
Let $\Upsilon_i(\varepsilon u)$ be the symbol for the parameter $u_\varepsilon$,
where $u_\varepsilon$ is the element of $\mathcal R_{\mathfrak c}$ 
congruent to $\varepsilon u$ mod $O_{\mathfrak c}$.
Then
\[
  \Upsilon_i(\varepsilon u)=\Upsilon_i(u)
  \quad\text{in}\quad H_1^!(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),A).
\]
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Put
$d_\varepsilon=
  \left(\begin{smallmatrix}\varepsilon&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and
$b=\varepsilon u-u_\varepsilon\in O_{\mathfrak c}$.
The diagonal matrices $d_\varepsilon$ and $t_i$ commute. Moreover,
\[
  d_\varepsilon t(u)=t(u_\varepsilon)
  \left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&b\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)d_\varepsilon
\]
and $d_\varepsilon$ normalizes $U_1^1(\mathfrak M)$.
It follows that
$d_\varepsilon\alpha_{u,i}d_\varepsilon^{-1}\in
t_it(u_\varepsilon)U_1^1(\mathfrak M)t_i^{-1}$
so we may choose
$\alpha_{\varepsilon u,i}
=d_\varepsilon\alpha_{u,i}d_\varepsilon^{-1}$ by 
remark~\ref{remark:automorphic-symbol-choice-independency}.
The definition of $\Delta_i$ gives a commutative
diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
E \arrow{r}{=} \arrow{d}{\Delta_i}
  & E \arrow{d}{\Delta_i} \\
Y^i(\mathfrak M)
\arrow{r}{d_\varepsilon^{\pm 1}} &
Y^i(\mathfrak M) .
\end{tikzcd}
\]
By the commutative diagram, it follows that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tr:unit:equiv}
\operatorname{Tr}_E\Delta_i^*(d_\varepsilon^*)^{\pm1}
=\operatorname{Tr}_E\Delta_i^*.  
\end{equation}

Now let $\eta\in H_!^1(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),A)$. As recalled in \S\ref{subsec:u0:u1}, the pullback to
$Y^i(\mathfrak N)$ of a cohomology class on $Y_1^i(\mathfrak N)$ is invariant under
the deck transformation $d_\varepsilon^*$. 
Since the matrices $d_\varepsilon$ and $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ commute,
we have \(d_\varepsilon^*\eta_{\mathrm c}=d_\varepsilon^*\mathcal E_q\eta'
=\mathcal E_qd_\varepsilon^*\eta'=\eta_{\mathrm c}.\)
Consequently, by~\eqref{eq:tr:unit:equiv},
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{Tr}_E\Delta_i^*\alpha_{\varepsilon u,i}^*
  \eta_{\operatorname c}
  &=
  \operatorname{Tr}_E\Delta_i^*(d_\varepsilon^*)^{-1}
  \alpha_{u,i}^*d_\varepsilon^*\eta_{\operatorname c}\\
  &=
  \operatorname{Tr}_E\Delta_i^*\alpha_{u,i}^*
  \eta_{\operatorname c}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, both symbols are constructed from the same functional using the fixed section \(s_M\).
So the assertion is true.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:parabolic-cohomology-base-change}
Assume that \(A\subset\mathbb C\) is a Dedekind domain. 
Then the coefficient-change map induces an isomorphism
\[
H_!^1(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),A)\otimes_A\mathbb C
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
H_!^1(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),\mathbb C).
\]
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Put $Y=Y_1^i(\mathfrak N)$, $H=H_!^1(Y,A)$, $M=H_1^!(Y,A)$, 
$H_{\mathbb C}=H_!^1(Y,\mathbb C)$ and $M_{\mathbb C}=H_1^!(Y,\mathbb C)$.
Set
\[
M^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,A),\qquad
M_{\mathbb C}^\vee
=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(M_{\mathbb C},\mathbb C).
\]
The coefficient-change map $H\longrightarrow H_{\mathbb C}$
induces the $\mathbb C$-linear map
\[
\beta_H:H\otimes_A\mathbb C\longrightarrow H_{\mathbb C}.
\]
By
Lemma~\ref{lem:parabolic-homology-base-change}, scalar extension
induces an isomorphism
\[
\beta_M:M\otimes_A\mathbb C
\xrightarrow{\;\simeq\;}M_{\mathbb C}.
\]
Write $T=M_{\mathrm{tors}}$ and $P=M/T$.
Since $M$ is finitely generated over the Dedekind domain $A$,
the module $P$ is finitely generated projective. Moreover,
\[
M^\vee=P^\vee,
\qquad
M\otimes_A\mathbb C=P\otimes_A\mathbb C.
\]
It follows that the natural map
$\Theta:M^\vee\otimes_A\mathbb C\longrightarrow M_{\mathbb C}^\vee$
defined by
\[
\Theta(\lambda\otimes z)
\left(\beta_M(m\otimes w)\right)
=zw\lambda(m)
\]
is an isomorphism.
We claim that the following diagram commutes:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
H\otimes_A\mathbb C
 \arrow{r}{\beta_H}
 \arrow{d}{\mathcal D_{\cap}\otimes 1}
&
H_{\mathbb C}
 \arrow{d}{\mathcal D_{\cap,\mathbb C}}
\\
M^\vee\otimes_A\mathbb C
 \arrow{r}{\Theta}
&
M_{\mathbb C}^\vee.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Indeed, for $\eta\in H$, $m\in M$, and $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
the naturality of the parabolic pairing gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal D_{\cap,\mathbb C}
\left(\beta_H(\eta\otimes z)\right)
\left(\beta_M(m\otimes w)\right)
&=
\beta_M(m\otimes w)\cap\beta_H(\eta\otimes z)\\
&=zw(m\cap\eta)\\
&=
\Theta\left(
\mathcal D_{\cap}(\eta)\otimes z
\right)
\left(\beta_M(m\otimes w)\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves the claim. By Lemma~\ref{dualmap:isom}, both vertical
maps are isomorphisms. Since $\Theta$ is also an isomorphism, the
commutative diagram shows that $\beta_H$ is an isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:additive-lvalue-automorphic-symbol}
For every
$f\in S_2(\mathfrak N,\chi)$ and $u\in\mathcal R_{\mathfrak c}$, we have
\[
\Upsilon_i(u)\cap\delta_i(f)
=\Gamma_F(1)L_{a_i}(1,\mathcal E_qf;u).
\]
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
By the definition of the automorphic symbol,
the Hecke equivariance of the generalized Eichler--Shimura map 
(Proposition~\ref{prop:eichler-shimura-u1-componentwise}),
the naturality of the parabolic pairing,
Lemma~\ref{lem:parabolic-cohomology-base-change},
and~\eqref{eq:hecke:section:compact:lifting},
we obtain
\[
\Upsilon_i(u)\cap\delta_i(f)
=\operatorname{Tr}_E\Delta_i^*\alpha_{u,i}^*
\iota_i\left(\delta_i(\mathcal E_qf)\right).
\]
Choose a differential form $\omega$ representing
$\delta_i(\mathcal E_qf)$. By the construction of section $\iota_i$ (see \S\ref{subsec:hecke:equiv:section}),
there is a function $\theta$, vanishing at the cusps,
such that
\[
\iota_i\left(\delta_i(\mathcal E_qf)\right)=[\omega-d\theta].
\]
From the defining property of $\alpha_{u,i}$ and the right invariance at
level $U_1^1(\mathfrak M)$, we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Tr}_E\Delta_i^*\alpha_{u,i}^*
\iota_i\left(\delta_i(\mathcal E_qf)\right)
&=
\int_E\Delta_i^*
\left(\alpha_{u,i}^*\omega-\alpha_{u,i}^*d\theta\right)=
\int_E\Delta_i^*\alpha_{u,i}^*\omega\\
&=
\int_E
\widetilde{((\mathcal E_qf)\vert_u)_{a_i}}(y)
\frac{dy}{y}.
\end{aligned}
\]
by Stokes' theorem.
Remark~\ref{rem:mellin-transform-extension} allows us to apply 
Proposition~\ref{integral:representation:lfunction} for $s=1$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{integral:lvalue:automorphic:symbol}
Suppose that \(A\subset\mathbb C\). Then, for every $f\in S_{2}(\mathfrak N,\chi)$, we have
\[
\Gamma_F(1)G(\xi)L_{a_i}(1,\mathcal E_qf\otimes\xi)
=
\xi(a_i)\sum_{u\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{c}}}
\xi(\varpi_\mathfrak{c}u)\Upsilon_i(u)\cap\delta_i(f).
\]
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:additive-lvalue-automorphic-symbol}, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\xi(a_i)\sum_u
\xi(\varpi_{\mathfrak c}u)
\Upsilon_i(u)\cap\delta_i(f)
&=
\Gamma_F(1)\xi(a_i)
\sum_u
\xi(\varpi_{\mathfrak c}u)
L_{a_i}(1,\mathcal E_qf;u).
\end{aligned}
\]
Then the assertion is true by Proposition~\ref{integral:representation:lfunction} 
and~\eqref{eq:twisting:class:character}.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:additive-average-symbols}
For an integer $n\geq n_0$ and elements $\alpha\in\mathfrak d_F^{-1}\setminus\{0\}$, 
$c\in O_\mathfrak{l}^\times$, define
\[
\Upsilon_c^n(\alpha):=\frac{\#E_F}{\ell^{n-n_0}}
\sum_{a\in c\Gamma_{n_0}/\Gamma_n}
\mathbf{e}_F\left(
-\frac{\alpha a}{\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^n}
\right)
\Upsilon_1\left(
\frac{a}{\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^n}
\right)\in H_1^!(Y_1^1(\mathfrak N),\mathbb C).
\]
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:automorphic-symbol-pairing-limit}
Let $0<e\leq 2n_0$ be an integer and set $\mathfrak{N}=\mathfrak l^e$.
For \(f\in \bigoplus_{\chi} S_2(\mathfrak l^e,\chi)\),
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\Upsilon_c^n(\alpha)\cap\delta_1(f)
=
\Gamma_F(1)\cdot\frac{a_{\mathcal E_qf}(\alpha \mathfrak d_F)}{N(\alpha \mathfrak d_F)}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Since the maps $f\mapsto a_{\mathcal E_qf}$ and $\delta_1$ are linear,
we may assume that $f\in S_2(\mathfrak l^e,\chi)$.
By Proposition~\ref{prop:additive-lvalue-automorphic-symbol}, we obtain
\[
\Upsilon_c^n(\alpha)\cap\delta_1(f)
=\# E_F \Gamma_F(1) L_n^{\mathrm{av}}(f;c,\alpha).
\]
Then Proposition~\ref{prop:additive-average-vertical-limit} gives the asserted limit.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
For an integral level $\mathfrak N$ and
$c\in O_{\mathfrak l}^{\times}$, define the $A$-submodule
\[
M_n^i(c):=
\operatorname{Span}_A
\left\{
  \Upsilon_i\left(\frac{a}{\varpi_\mathfrak{l}^n}\right):
  a\in c\Gamma_{n_0}
\right\}
\subset H_1^!(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),A).
\]
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:hecke-boundary-killing-operator-invertible}
$\mathcal E_q$ is invertible on the complex parabolic cohomology 
$H_!^1(Y_1(\mathfrak N),\mathbb{C})$.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
By the Hecke equivariance of the generalized Eichler--Shimura
isomorphism, it suffices to prove that $\mathcal E_q$ is invertible
on $S_2(\mathfrak N,\chi)$ for every $\chi$.

By~\cite{JacquetLanglands:1970}, 
the space $S_2(\mathfrak N,\chi)$ decomposes into its irreducible subspaces of cuspidal
automorphic forms. Since $\mathfrak q=q\mathcal O_F$ is prime
to $\mathfrak N$, 
                                                                        
                                                                         
$T_{\mathfrak q}$ acts on each summand by the multiplication by the Hecke eigenvalue $\lambda_f(\mathfrak q)$.
Put $Q=N(\mathfrak q)$. The bound of Blomer--Brumley~\cite{BlomerBrumley:2011} gives
\[
\left|\lambda_\pi(\mathfrak q)\right|
\leq 2Q^{1/2+\theta},
\qquad
\theta=\frac{7}{64}.
\]
Since $Q>1$ and $\theta<1/2$, we have
$\lambda_f(\mathfrak q)\neq Q+1$.
Thus $\mathcal E_q=T_{\mathfrak q}-Q-1$ acts on every automorphic
summand by a nonzero scalar. It is consequently invertible.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{vertical:direction}
Let $0<e\leq 2n_0$ be an integer and set $\mathfrak N=\mathfrak l^e$.
Fix $c\in O_{\mathfrak l}^{\times}$.
For all sufficiently large \(n\),
$M_n^1(c)$ is of full rank in
$H_1^!(Y_1^1(\mathfrak l^e),A)$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Assume the contrary.
Then there is a sequence $n_j\to\infty$ for which
\[
M_{n_j}^1(c)\otimes_A\mathbb C
\subsetneq H_1^!(Y_1^1(\mathfrak l^e),A)\otimes_A\mathbb C
\xrightarrow{\;\simeq\;}H_1^!(Y_1^1(\mathfrak l^e),\mathbb C),
\]
where the isomorphism is given by 
Lemma~\ref{lem:parabolic-homology-base-change}.
After passage to a subsequence,
\cite[Lemma~6.3]{Kwon:2023} gives a nonzero class
$\omega\in H_!^1(Y_1^1(\mathfrak l^e),\mathbb C)$ such that
\[
m_j\cap\omega\longrightarrow0
\]
for every bounded sequence
$m_j\in M_{n_j}^1(c)\otimes_A\mathbb C$. Write
$\omega=\delta_1(f)$ by
Proposition~\ref{prop:eichler-shimura-u1-componentwise}.
Let $\alpha\in \mathfrak d_F^{-1}\backslash\{0\}$.
By the definition,
\[
\Upsilon_c^{n_j}(\alpha)
\in M_{n_j}^1(c)\otimes_A\mathbb C.
\]
Choose cusp forms $\{g_r\}_r$ such that
$\{\delta_1(g_r)\}_r$ is a basis of $H^1_!(Y_1^1(\mathfrak l^e),\mathbb C)$. 
By the perfect pairing of Lemma~\ref{dualmap:isom} for $A=\mathbb C$, this fixed basis
defines a norm on $H_1^!(Y_1^1(\mathfrak N),\mathbb C)$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:automorphic-symbol-pairing-limit}
shows that, for every $r$, the sequence
$\{\Upsilon_c^{n_j}(\alpha)\cap\delta_1(g_r)\}_j$ converges.
This implies that $\{\Upsilon_c^{n_j}(\alpha)\}_j$ is bounded. 
The defining property of $\omega$ and Proposition~\ref{prop:automorphic-symbol-pairing-limit},
now applied to $f$, give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pairing:limit:vertical}
  0=
\lim_{j\to\infty}
\Upsilon_c^{n_j}(\alpha)\cap\delta_1(f)
 =\Gamma_F(1)\cdot
\frac{a_{\mathcal E_qf}(\alpha  \mathfrak d_F)}{N(\alpha \mathfrak d_F)}.
\end{equation}
Let us define the principal-class projector:
\[
P_1:S_2(\mathfrak l^e,\chi)\longrightarrow \sum_{\psi\in H_F}S_2(\mathfrak l^e,\chi\psi^2),\qquad
h\longmapsto\frac{1}{h_F}\sum_{\psi\in H_F}h\otimes\psi.
\]
Here, $H_F$ is the group of Hilbert characters.
Extend $P_1$ linearly to $\bigoplus_\chi S_2(\mathfrak l^e,\chi)$.
Since $\alpha$ was arbitrary, $P_1(\mathcal E_qf)=0$ by~\eqref{eq:pairing:limit:vertical}.
Therefore, we obtain 
\[
\delta_1(\mathcal E_qf)=\delta_1(P_1(\mathcal E_qf))=0.
\]
As $\delta$ is Hecke equivariant and 
$\mathcal E_q$ preserves the connected component,
Lemma~\ref{lem:hecke-boundary-killing-operator-invertible} now forces
$\omega=\delta_1(f)=0$, contradicting the choice of $\omega$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:automorphic-bianchi-comparison}
Let $u\in\mathcal R_{\mathfrak c}$. Then, in
$H_1^!(Y_1^1(\mathfrak N),A)$, one has
\begin{equation*}
\Upsilon_1(u)=\{r_u,\infty\}_1.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Set $\alpha_{u,1}:=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&r_u\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
By the choice of \(r_u\),
\[
\alpha_{u,1}\in
\mathrm{SL}_2(F)\cap
t(u)U_1^1(\mathfrak N\cap\mathfrak c^2).
\]
Thus $\alpha_{u,1}$ is an admissible choice in the definition of $\Upsilon_1(u)$.  
By Remark~\ref{remark:automorphic-symbol-choice-independency},
the symbol is independent of the choice of $\alpha_{u,1}$. Note that
\[
\alpha_{u,1}\circ\Delta_1
=\Delta_1^{r_u\to\infty}.
\]Thus \(\alpha_{u,1}\) translates the geodesic $\Delta_1(E)$ by \(r_u\).
Here $E\simeq\mathbb R_{>0}$ is oriented by $dy/y$, so the resulting
path runs from $r_u$ to $\infty$.
Therefore, for $\eta\in H_!^1(Y_1^1(\mathfrak N),A)$, we have
\[
\operatorname{Tr}_E\Delta_1^*
\alpha_{u,1}^*\eta_{\mathrm c}
=
\operatorname{Tr}_E
\bigl(\Delta_1^{r_u\to\infty}\bigr)^*\eta_{\mathrm c},
\]
which is the equality of the defining functionals of 
\(\Upsilon_1(u)\) and \(\{r_u,\infty\}_1\). This proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{full:rank:vertical}
There exist positive integers $n^\circ$ and $d^\circ$
such that, for every $c\in O_{\mathfrak l}^{\times}$, the module
$M_{n^\circ}^1(c)$ has full rank in
$H_1^!(Y_1^1(\mathfrak l^e),A)$ and
\[
M_{n^\circ}^1(c)\subset M_n^1(c)\quad\text{for every}\quad n\in n^\circ+d^\circ\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Let $L_0$ be the order of the group $(O_{\mathfrak l}/\mathfrak l^{n_0}O_{\mathfrak l})^\times$.
Since $M_n^1(c)$ depends only on $c$ mod $\mathfrak l^{n_0}$,
Theorem~\ref{vertical:direction} allows us to choose a sufficiently
large $r^\circ\geq e$, divisible by $L_0$, such that, for
$n^\circ=h_Fr^\circ$, every module $M_{n^\circ}^1(c)$ with
$c\in O_{\mathfrak l}^\times$ has full rank.

Choose a generator $\pi\in \mathcal O_F$ 
of the principal ideal $\mathfrak l^{h_F}$.
For $r\geq0$ and $\beta\in \mathcal O_F$ prime to $\mathfrak l$, let
$u_{\beta,r}\in\mathcal R_{\mathfrak l^{rh_F}}$ be the image of 
$\beta\pi^{-r}\in(\mathfrak l^{-rh_F}/\mathcal O_F)^\times$.
Then Theorem~\ref{thm:automorphic-bianchi-comparison} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:global-numerator-comparison}
\Upsilon_1(u_{\beta,r})
=\{\beta\pi^{-r},\infty\}_1.
\end{equation}
For each $c\in O_{\mathfrak l}^\times$, choose a set of representatives $B_c\subset \mathcal O_F$ of
\[
c\Gamma_{n_0}/\Gamma_{n^\circ}.
\]
Put $\mathcal B=\bigcup_{c\in(O_{\mathfrak l}/\mathfrak l^{n_0} O_{\mathfrak l})^\times}B_c$.
Let $D>0$ be a common multiple of $L_0$ and of the orders of $\pi$ in the finite groups
$(\mathcal O_F/\beta\mathcal O_F)^\times$
for all $\beta\in\mathcal B$. Fix $c\in O_{\mathfrak l}^\times$ and
choose $\beta\in B_c$, and $s\in D\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$. Set
\[
b=\beta\pi^{-r^\circ},
\qquad
g=\frac{\pi^{r^\circ}(\pi^s-1)}{\beta}.
\]
The factor $\pi^{r^\circ}$ is divisible by
$\mathfrak l^e$, whereas $\pi^s-1$ is divisible by
$\beta$.  Hence $\gamma_g:=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\g&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$
belongs to $\Gamma_1^1(\mathfrak l^e)$.  The relations
\eqref{eq:regularized-bianchi-relations} give
\begin{align*}
\{b,\infty\}_1
&=\gamma_g\{b,\infty\}_1
=\left\{\frac{b}{bg+1},\infty\right\}_1
  +\{\infty,0\}_1
  +\gamma_g\{0,\infty\}_1 \\
&=\left\{\beta\pi^{-(r^\circ+s)},\infty\right\}_1.
\end{align*}
Applying~\eqref{eq:global-numerator-comparison} to the above equation, we obtain
\[
\Upsilon_1(u_{\beta,r^\circ})
=
\Upsilon_1(u_{\beta,r^\circ+s})\quad\text{in}\quad H_1^!(Y_1^1(\mathfrak l^e),A).
\]
The element $u_{\beta,r}$ represents the same class as $\beta w^r/\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{rh_F}$, where
$
w=\pi^{-1}
\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{h_F}\in O_{\mathfrak l}^{\times}.
$
Since \(L_0\mid r^\circ\) and $s$, both \(w^{r^\circ}\) and
\(w^s\) belong to \(\Gamma_{n_0}\).
Consequently, 
\[
M_{n^\circ}^1(c)\subset M_{h_F(r^\circ+s)}^1(c)=M_{n^\circ+h_Fs}^1(c).
\]
Take $d^\circ=h_FD$, then this proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:vertical-full-rank-finite-field}
Let $B\subset\mathbb{C}$ be a Dedekind domain containing $A$.
Let $\mathfrak q$ be a prime ideal of $B$ such that $\mathfrak q\cap A$ is prime to
$\operatorname{Fitt}_A^0(\mathcal Q_c)$. Then, for any
$n\in\mathfrak V$, the inclusion induces an isomorphism
\[
M_n^1(c)\otimes_A B/\mathfrak q
\xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }
H_1^!(Y_1^1(\mathfrak N),B/\mathfrak q).
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Fix $c\in O_{\mathfrak l}^\times$ and put
\[
H_A:=H_1^!(Y_1^1(\mathfrak N),A),
\qquad
M^\circ:=M_{n^\circ}^1(c),
\qquad
\mathfrak{p}:=\mathfrak q\cap A,
\qquad
k=B/\mathfrak q.
\]
The assumption on $\mathcal Q_c$ implies
$(\mathcal Q_c)_{\mathfrak p}=0$.
Localizing the exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow M^\circ\longrightarrow H_A
\longrightarrow \mathcal Q_c
\longrightarrow0
\]
at $\mathfrak p$ gives the isomorphism
$
(M^\circ)_{\mathfrak p}\simeq(H_A)_{\mathfrak p}.
$
For every $n\in\mathfrak V$,
Theorem~\ref{full:rank:vertical} gives
\[
M^\circ\subset M_n^1(c)\subset H_A.
\]
After localization at \(\mathfrak p\), the two inclusions become
equalities.  Hence
$M_n^1(c)_{\mathfrak p}=(H_A)_{\mathfrak p}$.
Tensoring this equality over \(A_{\mathfrak p}\) with \(k\) gives
\[
M_n^1(c)\otimes_A k
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
H_A\otimes_A k.
\]
Finally,
Lemma~\ref{lem:parabolic-homology-base-change} identifies the
right-hand side with $H_1^!(Y_1^1(\mathfrak N),k)$. This proves the proposition.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:galois-average-reduction}
Assume that $n_0\geq r_\ell(\mathfrak p_0)$.
Then for every $\zeta\in\mu_{\ell^n}$ with $n\geq n_0$,
\[
 \frac{1}{\#D_n}\sum_{\tau\in D_n}\zeta^\tau
 \equiv
 \frac{1}{[\mathbb Q_n:\mathbb Q_{n_0}]}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb Q_n/\mathbb Q_{n_0})}\zeta^\sigma
 \pmod{\mathfrak p_n},
\]
where $D_n\subset \operatorname{Gal}(L_n/L_{n_0})$ is the decomposition group of $\mathfrak p_n$.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Let $\zeta\in\mu_{\ell^n}$.
Put $\lambda_n:=\mathcal O_{L_n}/\mathfrak p_n$. The action of $D_n$ on $\lambda_n$ induces a surjection
$
 D_n\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(\lambda_n/\lambda_{n_0}).
$
Consequently, compatibility of reduction with the Galois action gives
\[
 \frac{1}{\#D_n}\sum_{\tau\in D_n}\zeta^\tau
 \equiv
 \frac{1}{[\lambda_n:\lambda_{n_0}]}\operatorname{Tr}_{\lambda_n/\lambda_{n_0}}(\overline\zeta)
 \pmod{\mathfrak p_n}.
\]
Since $p\ne\ell$, reduction preserves the order of every
$\ell$-power root of unity. 
By the Lifting The Exponent lemma and our assumption on $n_0$, it follows that
\[
 \frac{1}{[\lambda_n:\lambda_{n_0}]}\operatorname{Tr}_{\lambda_n/\lambda_{n_0}}(\overline\zeta)
 =
 \begin{cases}
  \overline\zeta,&\zeta\in\mu_{\ell^{n_0}},\\
  0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
By~\eqref{eq:standard:cyclotomic:average}, the assertion is true.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{coates:wiles:extension}
For $n>0$, let us denote by $X_n$ the set of $\ell$-power order 
primitive Hecke characters of modulus $\mathfrak{l}^n$.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:prim:char:isom}
Let $n>1$ and $\phi\in X_n$. 
Then the restriction $\phi\vert_{\Gamma_1}$ gives a bijection 
between $X_n$ and the set of isomorphisms
$\Gamma_1/\Gamma_n\cong\mu_{\ell^{n-1}}$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
The restriction has kernel $\Gamma_n$ and inducesan isomorphism
as $\phi$ is primitive of modulus $\mathfrak l^n$ and is trivial on $\Delta$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:galois-average-residue-unit}
Let $\phi\in X_n$ and $a\in O_{\mathfrak l}^\times$.
Then,
\[
  \frac1{\#G_\phi}\sum_{\sigma\in G_\phi}\phi^\sigma(a)
  =
  \begin{cases}
    \displaystyle
    \phi(a)
    &
    \text{if }a\in W_\mathfrak{l}\Gamma_{n-n_0},
    \\
    0 & \text{otherwise}.
  \end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
The assertion follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:prim:char:isom} 
and the formula~\eqref{eq:standard:cyclotomic:average}.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:character-average}
For \(1\le i\le h_F\) and \(a\in O_{\mathfrak l}^{\times}\),
\[
  \frac{1}{\#\Delta}\sum_{\psi\in\widehat{\Delta}}
  \psi(aa_i)
  =
    \begin{cases}
    \displaystyle
    1, &
    \text{if }i=1\text{ and }a\in E_F\Gamma_1,\\
    0, & \text{otherwise},
  \end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
As $\psi$ is trivial on $\Gamma_1$, the average in the assertion is given by
$1$ if $\kappa a_i=1$ in $\Delta$ and $0$ otherwise,
where $\kappa\in W_{\mathfrak l}$ is the projection of $a$. 
$\kappa a_i=1$ if and only if $\kappa\in E_F$ and $i=1$ by~\eqref{fund:exact:seq:2}.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:average:lpower:l}
For \(1\le i\le h_F\), $\phi\in X_n$ and \(a\in O_{\mathfrak l}^{\times}\),
\[
\frac1{\# G_\phi}\sum_{\sigma\in G_\phi}\frac1{\#\Delta}\sum_{\psi\in\widehat\Delta}\phi^\sigma\psi(aa_i)=
\begin{cases}
\mathbf{e}_F\left(\frac{c_\phi(\kappa_a^{-1}a-1)}{\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{n}}\right)
& \text{if }i=1\text{ and }a\in E_F\Gamma_{n-n_0}, \\  
0 & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]
where $\kappa_a$ is the image of $a$ under the projection 
$O_{\mathfrak l}^\times\rightarrow W_{\mathfrak l}$.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
The assertion follows from the definition of $c_\phi$ 
and Lemmas~\ref{lem:galois-average-residue-unit} and~\ref{lem:character-average}.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lemma:integrality:cohomology:class}
Under the coefficient-change map for $Y_1^i(\mathfrak N)$ induced by $A\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$,
the image of \(\eta_{f,i,\mathrm c}\) is
$\varepsilon_q\frac{\iota_i(\delta_i(f))}{\Omega_f}$.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Choose a lift $\eta^\prime$ of $\eta_{f,i}$.
After changing of coefficients to $\mathbb{C}$, naturality of the maps in the
localization sequence gives the commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
H_c^1(Y_1^i(\mathfrak{N}),A) \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & 
H^1(Y_1^i(\mathfrak{N}),A) \arrow[d] \\
H_c^1(Y_1^i(\mathfrak{N}),\mathbb{C}) \arrow[r] & 
H^1(Y_1^i(\mathfrak{N}),\mathbb{C})
\end{tikzcd},\quad
\begin{tikzcd}
\eta^\prime \arrow[r, mapsto] & \eta_{f,i} \arrow[d, mapsto] \\
\frac{\iota_i(\delta_i(f))}{\Omega_f} \arrow[r, mapsto] & \frac{\delta_i(f)}{\Omega_f}
\end{tikzcd}.
\]
Consequently, the difference between the image of \(\eta^\prime\)
under coefficient change and
\(\iota_i(\delta_i(f))/\Omega_f\) lies in the image of
\[
H^0\left(\partial \overline{Y_1^i(\mathfrak N)}^{\mathrm BS},\mathbb C\right)
\longrightarrow
H_c^1(Y_1^i(\mathfrak N),\mathbb C).
\]
Lemma~\ref{hecke:action:boundary:cohom} shows that
\(\mathcal E_q\) annihilates this image. Since all the maps involved
are Hecke-equivariant, we obtain
\[
    \eta_{f,i,\operatorname{c}} = \mathcal{E}_q\eta^\prime
    \longmapsto\mathcal{E}_q\frac{\iota_i(\delta_i(f))}{\Omega_f}
    =
    \varepsilon_q \frac{\iota_i(\delta_i(f))}{\Omega_f}.
\]
This proves the lemma.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
Define the $L$-function of $f$ by
\[
L(s,f):=\sum_{\mathfrak{a}}\frac{a_f(\mathfrak{a})}{N(\mathfrak{a})^s},
\qquad\mathrm{Re}(s)>\frac{3}{2}+\theta,
\]
where $\mathfrak{a}$ runs through the non-zero integral ideals of $F$.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:eigenform-lvalue-automorphic-symbol}
If $f$ is a normalized Hecke eigenform, then
\[
\varepsilon_q L_f(\xi)=\sum_{i=1}^{h_F}
\xi(a_i)\sum_{u\in\mathcal R_{\mathfrak c}}
\xi(\varpi_{\mathfrak c}u)\Upsilon_i(u)\cap\eta_{f,i}.
\]
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Apply Proposition~\ref{integral:lvalue:automorphic:symbol} to
$f/\Omega_f$, noting that
$\frac{\delta_i(f)}{\Omega_f}=\eta_{f,i}$ and
$\mathcal E_qf=\varepsilon_qf$, then the assertion is true by the naturality of the pairing.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:gauss-inversion-fourier-operator}
Let $\xi$ be a primitive ray-class character of conductor
$\mathfrak l^{n_0}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gauss-inversion-full-fourier-operator}
\xi(a_i)\sum_{[g]\in(O_{\mathfrak l}/\mathfrak l^{n_0}O_{\mathfrak l})^\times/E_F}
\overline\xi(g)\mathcal F_{g,i}\eta_{f,i}
=G(\overline\xi)\overline\xi(d_F)\xi(d_{F,\mathfrak l})\mathcal R_i(\xi)\eta_{f,i}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Unfolding the definition of $\mathcal F_{g,i}$,
the left-hand side of~\eqref{eq:gauss-inversion-full-fourier-operator} is given by
\[
\xi(a_i)\sum_{b\ \mathrm{mod}\ \mathfrak l^{n_0}}
\left(
\sum_{g\in(O_{\mathfrak l}/\mathfrak l^{n_0}O_{\mathfrak l})^\times}
\overline\xi(g)
\mathbf e_F\left(
\frac{bg}{\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{n_0}}
\right)
\right)
\alpha_{b/\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^{n_0},i}^*\eta_{f,i}.
\]
Using inversion formula~\eqref{eq:gauss:inversion}, we are done.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:hecke-transport-twisted-class}
Let $\xi$ be a primitive finite-order Hecke character of conductor $\mathfrak l^{n_0}$. 
Then $\mathfrak J_{f,\xi}$ is a nonzero ideal of $B$.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Equation~\eqref{twisting:operators:compare} gives
\[
\mathcal R_1(\xi)\eta_{f,1}
=
\frac{G(\xi)}{\Omega_f}\delta_1(f\otimes\xi).
\]
Since $f$ is a normalized eigenform, $a_{f\otimes\xi}(\mathcal O_F)=1$, 
which implies that $\delta_1(f\otimes\xi)\neq 0$.
This proves the assertion together with Lemma~\ref{dualmap:isom}.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:residual-nonvanishing-eta-f}
Suppose that $\mathfrak q$ is prime to $\mathfrak J_f$.
Then there exists
$c\in O_{\mathfrak l}^\times$ such that
\[
\mathcal F_{c,1}\eta_{f,1}\ne0
\quad\text{in}\quad H_!^1(Y_1^1(\mathfrak N'),k').
\]
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
By assumption on $\mathfrak q$, 
we can choose a primitive finite order character $\xi$ of modulus $\mathfrak l^{n_0}$ such that
$\mathfrak J_{f,\xi}$ is coprime to $\mathfrak q$.
The definition of $\mathfrak J_{f,\xi}$ gives a class $m$ in
$H_1^!(Y_1^1(\mathfrak N'),B)$
such that
\[
m\cap\mathcal R_1(\xi)\eta_{f,1}\not\equiv0\pmod{\mathfrak q}.
\]
Naturality of the pairing implies
\[
\mathcal R_1(\xi)\eta_{f,1}\not\equiv0\pmod{\mathfrak q}.
\]
Since $p\ne\ell$, the Gauss sum $G(\overline\xi)$ is a
$\mathfrak q$-adic unit. Thus the reduction of
\eqref{eq:gauss-inversion-full-fourier-operator} has a nonzero
right-hand side. This proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:first-averaged-congruence}
Let $\phi\in X_n$ and $g_0\in O_{\mathfrak l}^{\times}$.
Assume that $\mathfrak p$ is coprime to $\#\Delta$.
If $n\geq 2n_0$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nonvanishing:lvalue}
\varepsilon_qL_f(\phi^\varepsilon\psi)\equiv0\pmod{\mathfrak P}
\end{equation}
for every $\psi\in\widehat\Delta$ and $\varepsilon \in E_F$, then
\begin{equation*}
\Upsilon_1
\left(\frac{g}{\varpi_{\mathfrak l}^n}\right)
\cap
\mathcal F_{c_\phi g_0^{-1},1}\eta_{f,1}
\equiv 0
\pmod{\mathfrak P}
\end{equation*}
for any $g\in g_0\Gamma_{n_0}$.
Here $\Upsilon_1$ is taken at level $\mathfrak N'$.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Let $g\in g_0\Gamma_{n_0}$. Put
\[
 G':=\operatorname{Gal}\left(
 L(\mu_{\ell^n})/
 L(\mu_{\ell^{n_0}})
 \right).
\]
Fix $\theta\in\{\phi^\varepsilon\}_{\varepsilon\in E_F}$.
The rationality of the algebraic $L$-values (Hida~\cite[\S8]{Hida:1994}) gives
\[
 L_f(\theta\psi)^\tau
 =L_f(\theta^\tau\psi)
 \qquad(\tau\in G').
\]
Apply Corollary~\ref{cor:eigenform-lvalue-automorphic-symbol} to~\eqref{eq:nonvanishing:lvalue}.
Take the average of the resulting equation twisted by $\theta^\tau\psi(g^{-1})$ over $\tau$ in the decomposition
group of $\mathfrak P$ in $G'$ and $\psi\in\widehat\Delta$. 
Lemma~\ref{lem:galois-average-reduction}
replaces the normalized decomposition-group average modulo
$\mathfrak P$ by the average for $G_\theta$. Thus, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:proof-prop106-character-average}
\begin{aligned}
 &\frac{1}{\#G_\theta}
 \sum_{\sigma\in G_\theta}
 \frac1{\#\Delta}
 \sum_{\psi\in\widehat\Delta}
 \sum_{i=1}^{h_F}\\
